newsitem.title: USA: Ford agrees to new settlement for Bronco II owners.
newsitem.headline: Ford agrees to new settlement for Bronco II owners.

text.p: Ford Motor Co. said Thursday it reached a new class-action settlement with owners of its controversial Bronco II sport utility vehicle that will provide new safety warnings and up to $200 for repairs and modifications.

The deal, which will be made available to about 658,000 Bronco II owners in the United States, replaces a settlement that was thrown out by a federal judge two years ago because of excessive attorneys fees.

U.S. District Judge Morey Sear in New Orleans, who will consider the new settlement, rejected the previous offer because he believed it gave Bronco owners "effectively zero" while giving plaintiff lawyers $4 million.

Ford for years has battled lawsuits alleging that the compact Bronco II is inherently prone to roll over because of its short wheelbase and high centre of gravity. Ford stopped producing the two-door Bronco II in 1990, but has vigorously defended the vehicle, blaming roll-overs on poor driving or unsafe modifications to the vehicles.
About 260 people have died in Bronco II roll-over crashes, and Sear in 1995 disclosed that Ford had paid $113 million to settle injury and wrongful death suits.

The new settlement, submitted to Sear on Tuesday, does not affect personal injury suits against Ford. Instead, it resolves class action claims that the alleged design defects reduced the vehicles' resale values.
Ford will provide owners with new warning labels, owners manuals and videocassettes that show situations in which sport utility vehicles can roll over, such as in sharp turns or abrupt manoeuvres.
Ford also will give owners $100 toward the cost of replacing worn-out shock absorbers and other suspension components. Ford also will pay up to $200 to owners who make certain modifications.

"The settlement agreement reiterates a message that we've communicated for years, that the Bronco II is a safe vehicle when driven with common sense and accordance with safe driving practices," said Ford spokeswoman Jennifer Flake.
She declined to specify the overall cost of the settlement to Ford and added that the automaker has not agreed to any specified level of attorneys fees in the deal.
Plaintiff lawyers have said in court documents that they will seek less than $6 million in fees from Ford, but the final amount will be determined by Sear.
